description: End-to-end production system design blueprints following the 7-step framework: 1. Requirement Gathering, 2. Scale Assumption, 3. QPS/Memory/5-Year Storage Estimation, 4. subtopics.title: URL Shortener
subtopics.subtitle: Bitly-scale URL shortening and redirection: Base62 encoding, range-allocated ID generation, and sub-10ms edge redirects.
keyTakeaways: A 7-character Base62 string ([0-9a-zA-Z]) provides 62^7 = 3.52 trillion unique aliases: enough for a century of traffic at 1,000 writes/second with zero collision risk.
Pre-allocating ID ranges using etcd or ZooKeeper leases leases blocks of numeric IDs to application servers in memory, eliminating write-time database round-trips and collision retries.
HTTP 301 offloads redirection to browser and CDN caches to minimize origin load, but blinds server-side analytics. HTTP 302 forces requests through your proxy, enabling real-time telemetry.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A URL Shortener turns long URLs into compact aliases (e.g., `https://sho.rt/7kL9xQ`) and redirects incoming requests to the destination with low latency.
bullets: Functional: Generate a unique 7-character Base62 code for any valid long URL; support optional custom aliases (up to 16 chars) and configurable expiration TTLs.
Functional: Redirect `GET /{shortCode}` to the target destination via HTTP 301 or 302, returning HTTP 404 or 410 if expired or not found.
Functional: Asynchronously record click analytics (timestamp, referrer, country, user agent) without stalling the redirect critical path.
Non-Functional: Redirection p99 latency under 10ms within the data center, and under 40ms globally via CDN edge caching.
Non-Functional: High read availability (99.99%). A transient database partition must never break redirects for existing cached URLs.
Out of Scope: Real-time user billing, malicious destination malware scanning pipelines, and link preview scrapers.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: URL shorteners are heavily read-skewed. Sizing the architecture requires understanding the 100:1 read-to-write ratio and diurnal traffic patterns.
bullets: Write Volume: 100 million new URLs created per month (~40 writes/second average, peaking at 200 writes/second).
Read Volume: 10 billion redirects per month (~4,000 reads/second average, peaking at 15,000 to 20,000 reads/second during viral campaigns).
Storage Footprint: Average URL record is ~500 bytes (original URL, short code, user ID, creation date, TTL). 100 million URLs/month * 500 bytes = 50 GB/month, or 3 TB across 5 years.
Cache Working Set: By the 80/20 rule, 20% of popular links drive 80% of click traffic. Caching 20% of a day's read traffic in memory requires roughly 30 to 40 GB of Redis RAM.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Storage capacity is rarely the constraint in a URL shortener; network bandwidth, connection handling, and memory cache hit ratio drive system performance.
bullets: Base62 address space: Using characters [0-9, a-z, A-Z] gives 62 characters. At 7 characters, 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 unique URLs (~3.52 trillion).
Read throughput sizing: 20,000 peak QPS * 500 bytes per redirect response = ~10 MB/s of outbound network bandwidth, which easily fits within standard cloud instances.
Cache memory sizing: 20% of 330 million daily requests = 66 million unique URLs cached * 500 bytes = 33 GB of RAM for a 90%+ cache hit ratio.

================================================================================
                  URL SHORTENER CAPACITY ESTIMATION SHEET
================================================================================
1. TRAFFIC & QPS (1 Day = 86,400 seconds ≈ 100,000 seconds)
   - Daily Writes (New URLs)    : 100,000,000 (100M / day)
   - Average Write QPS          : 100M / 86,400      = ~1,160 QPS
   - Peak Write QPS (3x)        : 1,160 * 3          = ~3,500 QPS
   - Daily Reads (Redirects)    : 10,000,000,000 (10B / day, 100:1 ratio)
   - Average Read QPS           : 10B / 86,400       = ~115,740 QPS
   - Peak Read QPS (3x)         : 115,740 * 3        = ~350,000 QPS

2. SHORT CODE KEYSPACE MATH (Base62 = [0-9, a-z, A-Z])
   - 6 characters : 62^6 = 56.8 Billion unique keys
   - 7 characters : 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208 (3.52 Trillion unique keys)
   - Required for 5 years       : 100M/day * 365 * 5 = 182.5 Billion URLs
   -> Decision: 7-char Base62 provides ~19x headroom over 5-year requirement.

3. 5-YEAR PERSISTENT STORAGE
   - Record Size                : ~600B payload + ~400B index/metadata = 1 KB
   - Total Records (5 Years)    : 1.825 * 10^11 records (182.5B)
   - Raw Storage                : 182.5B * 1 KB      = 182.5 TB
   - Replicated Storage (RF=3)  : 182.5 TB * 3       = 547.5 TB (~550 TB)

4. REDIS CACHE MEMORY (RAM)
   - Daily Hot Set (20% of 100M): 20M keys * 1 KB    = 20 GB RAM
   - 30-Day Hot Working Set     : 600M keys * 1 KB   = 600 GB RAM
   - Cluster Topology           : 10 Primary + 10 Replica nodes (64 GB RAM each)

5. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Ingress (Write)       : 3,500 QPS * 1 KB   = 3.5 MB/sec  (28 Mbps)
   - Peak Egress (Read)         : 350,000 QPS * 1 KB = 350 MB/sec  (2.8 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Keep the API surface minimal and deterministic. Separate URL creation from public redirection to avoid contention between administrative endpoints and the hot redirect path.
bullets: Write API: `POST /api/v1/urls` takes `{ longUrl, customAlias?, ttlSeconds? }` and returns `{ shortUrl, shortCode, expiresAt }`.
Read API: `GET /{shortCode}` returns a 301/302 Redirect with a `Location: <longUrl>` header, or a 404/410 status code.
Schema: Store records in a distributed key-value store (DynamoDB or Cassandra) partitioned by `short_code`, indexing `created_at` for background TTL cleanup.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: We decouple the Write Path (ID generation and persistence) from the Read Path (cached redirection) so viral traffic spikes on existing links never degrade link creation.
bullets: Edge CDN: Caches permanent 301 redirects close to users, answering repeated viral clicks without hitting your origin cluster.
ID Allocator (etcd / ZooKeeper): Leases non-overlapping numeric ID blocks (e.g., 100,000 IDs at a time) to application server instances in memory.
Redirect Service: Stateless service querying local Caffeine L1 cache and Redis L2 cluster. If a key misses, it reads DynamoDB and populates the cache.
Asynchronous Analytics: Emits click metadata to Kafka; a streaming worker (Flink or Spark) aggregates hourly metrics into ClickHouse.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: The central engineering problem in a URL shortener is generating collision-free short codes without taking database row locks on every write.
bullets: Why hashing fails: Taking MD5/SHA-256 of `longUrl` and truncating to 7 characters produces birthday-paradox hash collisions as the database grows, requiring check-and-retry database loops.

Range-based counters: An etcd or ZooKeeper cluster maintains a global monotonic counter. Each app server grabs a range (e.g., Server A gets 1,000,000–1,999,999). When a write arrives, Server A increments its local memory counter and converts the integer directly to Base62. Zero network calls, zero collisions.
Handling custom aliases: If a user specifies a custom alias, bypass the range counter and perform a conditional `INSERT ... IF NOT EXISTS` against the database to guarantee uniqueness.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Protecting the redirect path against cold starts, cache avalanches, and malicious links is what separates toy projects from production infrastructure.
bullets: Bloom filters for nonexistent links: Attackers scanning random 7-character URLs can cause a cache-penetration storm against the primary database. Place a Bloom filter in front of the database to discard 99% of invalid keys instantly.
Cache stampede mitigation: Use Singleflight request coalescing in application memory so 10,000 concurrent requests for an expired viral link trigger only one database read.
Async click ingestion: Never execute click logging synchronously in the redirect handler. Write click events to a non-blocking in-memory ring buffer that flushes to Kafka asynchronously.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees zero collisions; no database read before write; deterministic 7-character length.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires managing a consensus cluster; sequential numbers can be guessed unless randomized via a bit-shuffling feistel cipher.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput enterprise shorteners (Bitly, TinyURL) requiring high write efficiency.

tradeOffs.pros: Stateless; identical URLs naturally map to the same short code without central coordination.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires check-then-set database round-trips to detect collisions; write latency degrades as database fills.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-scale internal link shorteners where identical links must be deduplicated automatically.

tradeOffs.pros: 301 allows browser and CDN edge caching, delivering sub-5ms redirects with zero server load.
tradeOffs.cons: 301 prevents the origin from capturing click analytics on subsequent visits and makes URL target changes difficult.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Use 301 for static promotional links; use 302 when detailed click attribution or retargeting is required.

subtopics.interviewTip: Do not suggest MD5 truncation without discussing the birthday paradox. Walk the interviewer through Base62 range leases: explain how etcd allocates blocks of 100,000 IDs to app servers in memory, eliminating write-path database contention, and contrast HTTP 301 vs 302.

subtopics.title: E-commerce Order System
subtopics.subtitle: E-commerce order processing: Saga orchestration, striped inventory reservation, and immutable price snapshots.
keyTakeaways: Coordinate distributed order checkout across Order, Inventory, Payment, and Shipping services using a stateful Saga Orchestrator with explicit compensating transactions (releaseInventory, refundPayment): avoid distributed XA two-phase commits.
Record an immutable snapshot of item title, seller ID, unit price, tax rate, and applied discounts inside order_items at the exact moment of checkout so future catalog edits never mutate past orders.

Eliminate database row-lock contention on hot flash-sale items by striping inventory across K database sub-buckets (sku_id#00 through sku_id#63) combined with an atomic Redis token pre-reservation check.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: An E-Commerce Order System coordinates checkout transactions across distributed services, ensuring reliable inventory reservation, payment capture, and order tracking.
bullets: Functional: Create orders from a shopping cart; reserve and decrement inventory atomically; coordinate payment capture; handle order cancellation and compensation.
Functional: View order history with immutable pricing and tax details; track shipment status.
Non-Functional: High consistency on checkout (never sell more units than physically exist in inventory).
Non-Functional: Support high-concurrency flash sales (e.g., 50,000 checkout attempts/second on a single hot item).
Out of Scope: Warehouse logistics robot pathfinding, personalized product recommendation models, and delivery driver dispatch.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: E-commerce platforms operate under steady baseline traffic punctuated by extreme flash-sale spikes.
bullets: Baseline Volume: 5 million orders placed per day (~60 orders/second average, peaking at 500 orders/sec).
Flash Sale Peak: Limited-release product launches generate 50,000 checkout requests/second targeting the same SKU.
Order Record Size: Average order with items, addresses, and line-item tax details is ~2 KB. 5 million orders/day = 10 GB/day of data.
Consistency Requirement: Zero overselling. Strict inventory bounds must be enforced across concurrent buyers.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Capacity bottlenecks in checkout systems are driven by database row-level locking on inventory tables rather than disk space.
bullets: Row-lock concurrency limit: In PostgreSQL or MySQL, updating a single inventory row (`UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE sku_id = X`) acquires an exclusive row lock. A single database row can only process 1,000 to 2,000 updates/second before lock wait timeouts collapse the database.
Flash-sale shortfall: Handling 50,000 requests/second on a single SKU requires a 25x improvement over single-row lock throughput, mandating Redis pre-reservation or inventory striping.
Storage durability: 10 GB/day * 365 days = 3.65 TB/year of relational order history, easily managed with partitioned tables in PostgreSQL.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: APIs must require client idempotency keys to protect against duplicate orders during network retries.
bullets: Create Order API: `POST /v1/orders/checkout` takes `{ idempotencyKey, cartId, shippingAddressId, paymentMethodId }` and returns `{ orderId, status: "PROCESSING" }`.
Order Schema: `orders` table (`order_id`, `user_id`, `total_amount`, `status`, `created_at`) with foreign keys to `order_items`.

Immutable Price Snapshot: `order_items` stores copies of `unit_price`, `title`, `tax_rate`, and `discount_amount` captured at the time of purchase, preventing future catalog updates from corrupting historical orders.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The checkout architecture uses an orchestrator-driven Saga pattern to manage distributed state across services.
bullets: Order Service: Ingests checkout requests, validates idempotency keys, records the pending order, and initializes the Saga.
Saga Orchestrator (Temporal / Step Functions): Executes sequential steps across services (Reserve Inventory -> Capture Payment -> Confirm Order), executing compensating actions if any step fails.
Inventory Service: Manages stock levels using Redis token buckets for pre-reservation and striped relational tables for durable persistence.
Payment Gateway Adapter: Communicates with external payment processors outside the database transaction.
Transactional Outbox: Ensures events are published to Kafka reliably alongside database state changes.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Coordinating checkout across independent microservices requires handling partial failures gracefully without distributed locks.
bullets: The Saga execution sequence: 1. Create order in `PENDING` state. 2. Reserve stock in Inventory Service. 3. Authorize and capture payment. 4. Update order to `CONFIRMED`.

Compensating on payment failure: If payment authorization fails in step 3, the orchestrator invokes the compensation step on the Inventory Service (`releaseInventory(orderId)`), returning stock to the available pool.

Inventory striping for flash sales: Divide inventory for SKU X into 32 sub-buckets (`sku_X_0` to `sku_X_31`), each holding a fraction of the total stock. Incoming checkouts pick a bucket randomly (`hash(userId) % 32`), distributing row locks across 32 separate database records.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Flash-sale resilience requires protecting databases from thundering-herd checkout traffic.
bullets: Redis pre-reservation with Lua scripts: Check and decrement stock in Redis before writing to the database. If Redis stock reaches zero, reject excess checkout attempts immediately with HTTP 409 (Sold Out), sparing the database.

Idempotency state machine: Store idempotency keys in Redis with status `IN_PROGRESS`, `SUCCESS`, or `FAILED`. If a client retries while an order is processing, return a `409 Conflict` or poll for completion.
Reconciliation cron workers: Run hourly reconciliation jobs that compare inventory reservation logs against confirmed orders to release abandoned or orphaned stock locks.

tradeOffs.pros: Clear end-to-end visibility of transaction state; easy to monitor, debug, and enforce timeouts.
tradeOffs.cons: The orchestrator service is a critical component that requires high availability and durability.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Complex multi-step e-commerce checkouts involving inventory, billing, tax, and shipping.

tradeOffs.pros: Decoupled services; no single orchestrator bottleneck; services listen to domain events independently.
tradeOffs.cons: Hard to trace the complete workflow during incidents; risk of cyclic event dependencies and difficult compensations.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Simple, loosely coupled 2-step workflows like sending a confirmation email after signup.

tradeOffs.option: Striped Database Inventory vs Redis Pre-Reservation
tradeOffs.pros: Redis pre-reservation absorbs 50,000 QPS with sub-millisecond latency; striped DB rows provide durable persistence.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires keeping Redis and database stock synchronized; potential for drift during Redis crash recovery.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-concurrency ticket drops, smartphone launches, and viral flash-sale platforms.

subtopics.interviewTip: Do not use distributed 2-Phase Commit (XA) across microservices—explain that network partitions lock database tables and degrade availability. Propose an Orchestrated Saga with explicit compensating actions, and describe inventory striping to solve single-row database lock contention during flash sales.

subtopics.title: Uber / Ride Matching
subtopics.subtitle: Real-time ride dispatching: H3 hexagonal spatial indexing, route-network ETA calculation, and transactional driver locking.
keyTakeaways: Partition geospatial coordinates into Uber H3 hexagonal cells (Resolution 8 ~ 0.73 km², Resolution 9 ~ 0.1 km²): hexagons provide equal distances to all 6 neighbors, eliminating edge and corner distortion found in rectangular grids.
Decouple high-frequency ephemeral driver location pings (stored in memory in Redis Geo/H3 clusters) from durable trip state machines (persisted in PostgreSQL/CockroachDB with optimistic locking).

Rank candidate drivers using actual road-network driving ETAs (Dijkstra or Contraction Hierarchies with live traffic) rather than straight-line Euclidean distance, and acquire distributed locks on candidate drivers during dispatch offers.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A Real-Time Ride Matching System tracks moving drivers, matches rider pickup requests to optimal nearby drivers, and manages trip lifecycles from dispatch to drop-off.
bullets: Functional: Drivers periodically report GPS locations (every 3-5 seconds); riders request pickups; match riders to the nearest available driver based on driving ETA; track trip status.
Functional: Real-time driver location updates on the rider's map.
Non-Functional: Match completion latency under 3 seconds; sub-second location ingestion.
Non-Functional: Zero double-booking: a driver must never be successfully dispatched to two riders simultaneously.
Out of Scope: Dynamic surge pricing economic algorithms, turn-by-turn navigation voice synthesis, and driver document verification.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Ride-matching architectures are characterized by massive write volumes from moving drivers and compute-intensive routing calculations.
bullets: Active Fleet: 1 million active drivers reporting GPS coordinates every 4 seconds = 250,000 location updates/second.
Rider Demand: 10 million completed trips per day (~120 ride requests/second average, peaking at 1,500 requests/second during peak hours).
Location Payload: 32 bytes per ping (`driver_id`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `bearing`, `timestamp`). 250,000 pings/sec = ~8 MB/s of ingress network stream.
Candidate Search Fan-Out: Each ride request evaluates the nearest 20 to 50 candidate drivers within a 3 to 5 km radius.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Calculating location stream throughput demonstrates why location pings must be processed in memory rather than persisted directly to disk.
bullets: Database write bottleneck: 250,000 writes/second would overwhelm traditional relational databases with disk I/O. In-memory data structures (Redis Geo or custom H3 memory indexes) are required for location tracking.
Memory sizing for location state: 1 million active drivers * 128 bytes metadata in Redis = ~128 MB of RAM, easily fitting on a single Redis master (sharded for network throughput).
ETA computation budget: 1,500 peak ride requests/sec * 30 candidate drivers evaluated = 45,000 routing graph calculations per second, mandating pre-computed Contraction Hierarchies.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Driver location updates use lightweight UDP or WebSocket streams, while rider requests use REST/gRPC endpoints.
bullets: Driver Location Ping: WebSocket/gRPC streaming frame: `{ driverId, lat, lon, bearing, status: "AVAILABLE"|"ON_TRIP", timestamp }`.
Ride Request API: `POST /v1/rides/request` takes `{ riderId, pickupLat, pickupLon, dropoffLat, dropoffLon }` and returns `{ tripId, status: "SEARCHING" }`.
Data Storage: Driver locations stored in in-memory H3 spatial indexes; trip records stored in PostgreSQL with state machines (`REQUESTED`, `MATCHED`, `ARRIVED`, `IN_TRANSIT`, `COMPLETED`).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture cleanly separates high-throughput location ingestion from trip state orchestration and routing calculation engines.
bullets: Location Ingestion Fleet: Terminates driver WebSocket connections and updates the in-memory spatial index.
Spatial Index (Uber H3 / Redis Geo): Sharded in-memory index mapping H3 hexagon cells to lists of active available driver IDs.
Dispatch Orchestrator: Receives ride requests, queries H3 for candidate drivers, calculates road ETAs, and manages dispatch offers.
Routing & ETA Engine: Graph-processing service running Contraction Hierarchies with live traffic speed matrices.
Trip State Service: Durable relational database managing the official trip lifecycle with optimistic concurrency control.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Matching a rider to a driver involves spatial indexing, candidate pruning, routing calculation, and atomic driver locking.
bullets: H3 Spatial Indexing: Map the rider's pickup coordinates to an H3 Resolution 8 hexagon. Query the home hexagon and its 6 immediate neighbors (`kRing(1)`), retrieving all available driver IDs within ~1.5 km.

Road-network ETA calculation: Do not rank candidates by straight-line Euclidean distance (which ignores rivers, one-way streets, and highways). Use pre-computed Contraction Hierarchies to compute real driving travel times for the top 20 candidates.

Two-phase dispatch offer and locking: Acquire a distributed Redis lock on the highest-ranked driver (`SET lock:driver:{id} {tripId} NX EX 15`). Push the dispatch offer to the driver's phone with a 15-second countdown. If the driver accepts, transition trip state to `MATCHED`; if they reject or time out, release the lock and offer to candidate #2.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Handling network disconnections, stale GPS readings, and sudden regional traffic spikes is required for platform stability.
bullets: Stale location expiration: Expire driver locations automatically if no ping is received for 15 seconds. If a driver loses cellular connection in a tunnel, they drop out of candidate pools immediately rather than receiving failed dispatch offers.

Batch dispatching (Bipartite Matching): In dense city centers, sequential dispatching can lead to suboptimal assignments. Collect ride requests in 3-second windows and solve matching as a Global Bipartite Matching problem (Hungarian algorithm) to minimize aggregate waiting time.

Preventing race conditions on acceptance: If two dispatch workers attempt to offer the same driver simultaneously, the Redis `SET NX` lock ensures exactly one succeeds while the other falls back to alternative candidates.

tradeOffs.pros: All 6 adjacent cells are equidistant; uniform neighbor expansion; smooth hierarchical resolutions.
tradeOffs.cons: Slightly higher compute overhead than rectangular Geohashes; requires custom coordinate conversion libraries.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Real-time dispatch systems, ride-sharing, food delivery, and dynamic geographic zone partitioning.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple string prefix queries (e.g., SQL `WHERE geohash LIKE "9q8yy%"`); widely supported out of the box.
tradeOffs.cons: Severe distortion at high latitudes; corners of a square are 1.414x further away than edge centers, creating directional bias.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Static location lookups like "find coffee shops near me" or Yelp-style business directories.

tradeOffs.option: Road-Network Contraction Hierarchies vs Euclidean Distance
tradeOffs.pros: Accurate ETAs accounting for one-way streets, bridges, and traffic jams; prevents assigning drivers across rivers.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires maintaining and regularly updating heavy road graph data in memory.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Ride-sharing dispatch, emergency vehicle dispatch, and courier delivery routing.

Describe the dispatch flow: query H3 k-ring for candidate drivers, rank by road-network ETA, and acquire a temporary distributed lock on the driver during the 15-second acceptance window.

subtopics.title: Stock Trading System
subtopics.subtitle: Ultra-low-latency electronic exchange: LMAX Disruptor, deterministic single-threaded matching, and Raft journaling.
keyTakeaways: Never use database locks or multi-threaded mutexes inside a Limit Order Book (LOB): partition matching engines by symbol and run each symbol on a single pinned CPU core using an LMAX Disruptor lock-free ring buffer.

Achieve high availability through Deterministic State Machine Replication: sequence every incoming order through a Raft-replicated append-only journal so standby replicas reconstruct the exact same order book in microseconds.

Model price levels using a dual data structure: a TreeMap (or flat array indexed by price tick) for O(1) best bid/ask lookups, paired with doubly-linked lists of orders at each price level for O(1) FIFO time-priority matching and O(1) order cancellation.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: An Electronic Stock Trading Exchange matches buyers and sellers in real time based on Price-Time Priority (FIFO), maintaining deterministic order books and sub-millisecond execution latencies.
bullets: Functional: Place, cancel, and modify Limit and Market orders; match compatible bids and asks according to Price-Time Priority; broadcast real-time market data (Level 2 order books and execution trades).
Functional: Pre-trade risk checks (verifying margin and available cash before an order reaches the matching engine).
Non-Functional: Deterministic sub-millisecond matching latency (p99 < 500 microseconds inside the matching core).
Non-Functional: Strict FIFO fairness: orders at the same price must execute strictly in the order they arrived at the exchange.
Non-Functional: High durability: zero lost executions once acknowledged to the broker.
Out of Scope: Options/futures derivative pricing models, high-frequency market-making proprietary trading algorithms, and multi-currency clearinghouse settlement.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Electronic exchanges handle intense message throughput during market open and close auctions, characterized by high cancellation-to-trade ratios.
bullets: Order Throughput: 100,000 orders and cancels per second across the exchange, peaking at 500,000 ops/second during market open.
Order-to-Trade Ratio: In modern electronic markets, 95% of orders are cancels or price adjustments placed by algorithmic market makers; only ~5% result in executed trades.
Symbol Cardinality: 10,000 active stock tickers, with 80% of volume concentrated in the top 200 liquid symbols (e.g., AAPL, NVDA, SPY).
Latency Budget: Ingress gateway pre-trade risk check < 100us; matching engine execution < 50us; journaling < 200us.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Capacity in a trading engine is measured in nanoseconds of CPU execution time and network packet transmission rather than terabytes of disk.
bullets: Matching engine budget: 50,000 orders/sec on a single hot symbol means the matching engine has an upper bound of 20 microseconds per order. Multi-threaded locking overhead (mutex lock/unlock takes 50-100ns plus context switch costs) makes locks unacceptable.
Journal storage: 500,000 orders/sec * 128 bytes per binary order record = ~64 MB/s of sequential append-only disk write, easily handled by high-end NVMe SSDs.
Market data broadcast bandwidth: 50,000 matched trades/sec * 64 bytes binary UDP multicast packet = ~3.2 MB/s outbound multicast stream.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Financial exchanges communicate using high-performance binary protocols (like Simple Binary Encoding / SBE) or standard FIX (Financial Information eXchange) over TCP.
bullets: New Order Single (FIX 4.4 / SBE): Message containing `ClOrdID`, `Symbol`, `Side` (`BUY`|`SELL`), `OrderQty`, `Price`, `OrdType` (`LIMIT`|`MARKET`), `TimeInForce`.
Execution Report: Broadcasts `ExecID`, `OrderID`, `ExecType` (`NEW`|`TRADE`|`CANCELED`), `LastShares`, `LastPx`, `LeavesQty`.
In-Memory Limit Order Book: `Order` struct (`order_id`, `price`, `quantity`, `timestamp`, `prev`, `next`), `PriceLevel` struct (`price`, `total_volume`, `head_order`, `tail_order`).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The trading platform follows the LMAX architecture: a sequenced input pipeline feeding a deterministic, single-threaded in-memory matching core.
bullets: FIX / SBE Gateway: Terminates broker TCP connections, authenticates sessions, and decodes binary packets.
Pre-Trade Risk Engine: In-memory validator ensuring the broker has sufficient margin and has not breached risk limits.
Sequencer & Replicated Journal (Aeron / Raft): Assigns a strict monotonic sequence number to every order and writes to an append-only log across 3 nodes before matching.
Single-Threaded Matching Engine: Consumes sequenced orders from an in-memory lock-free ring buffer (LMAX Disruptor) and updates the in-memory order book.
Market Data Publisher: Broadcasts matched trade feeds and Level 2 depth via UDP Multicast to market participants.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Executing trades with deterministic microsecond latency requires single-threaded memory processing paired with dual data structures.
bullets: Why single-threaded beats multi-threaded: Shared-memory concurrency with mutexes or read-write locks causes CPU cache line bouncing and OS thread context switching. Running the matching engine on a single CPU core pinned with `taskset` eliminates lock contention and achieves predictable execution.

Order book data structure: Maintain two side structures: Bids (sorted descending) and Asks (sorted ascending). Use a B-tree or array of price ticks for $O(1)$ lookup of the best bid/ask, and a doubly-linked list of orders at each price level to enforce FIFO execution.

Order cancellation in O(1): Maintain an in-memory hash map of `order_id -> OrderNode*`. To cancel an order, look up the node in $O(1)$, unlink it from the doubly-linked list in $O(1)$, and decrement the price level volume.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Exchanges must guarantee state reproducibility and instantaneous failover without losing a single trade.
bullets: Deterministic state machine replay: Because the matching engine is single-threaded and deterministic, feeding the exact same sequence of input events into an empty engine produces the exact same order book state. If the primary crashes, a warm standby reading the Raft journal takes over in microseconds.

Memory pre-allocation and zero GC: In Java/C++, allocate all order objects in pre-sized memory pools at startup. Never allocate objects on the heap during active trading hours to prevent garbage collection pauses from halting the matching loop.

Kernel bypass networking: Use Solarflare OpenOnload or DPDK to read network packets directly from the network interface card (NIC) into application memory, bypassing the Linux kernel network stack and shaving 5 to 10 microseconds off ingress latency.

tradeOffs.option: Single-Threaded Pinned Core with LMAX Disruptor
tradeOffs.pros: Deterministic microsecond latency; zero lock contention; zero thread context switches; clean FIFO ordering.
tradeOffs.cons: Throughput per symbol is bound by the clock speed of a single CPU core; requires partitioning symbols across cores.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Electronic exchanges (NASDAQ, LMAX, CME), crypto matching engines, and high-frequency trading platforms.

tradeOffs.option: Multi-Threaded Order Book with Fine-Grained Locks
tradeOffs.pros: Can leverage multiple CPU cores across a single symbol's price levels.
tradeOffs.cons: Lock contention, cache line bouncing, and non-deterministic execution times under high volatility.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Low-frequency trading platforms or internal crossing networks with modest throughput.

tradeOffs.pros: Cuts network latency from 15 microseconds down to 1.5 microseconds by bypassing OS socket layers.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires specialized network hardware, dedicated CPU polling cores, and complex low-level C/C++ driver code.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Tier 1 electronic exchanges and algorithmic trading firms competing on speed.

subtopics.interviewTip: When asked how an exchange handles high throughput, immediately explain why you do NOT use database transactions or multi-threaded locks. Propose the LMAX architecture: partition by symbol, run each symbol's order book single-threaded on a dedicated CPU core using lock-free ring buffers, and replicate state via a deterministic append-only journal.

subtopics.title: Distributed Job Scheduler
subtopics.subtitle: Cloud-scale distributed job scheduling: time-bucketed sharding, hierarchical timing wheels, and fencing-token leases.
keyTakeaways: Partition schedule scanning by (time_bucket_minute, shard_id) so schedule pollers perform sequential partition scans on the current minute window rather than executing expensive unindexed range queries across billions of future jobs.

Bridge the gap between minute-level database buckets and sub-second execution precision using an in-memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel (HashedWheelTimer) before dispatching ready tasks to worker queues.

Protect against worker crashes using Lease Expirations (visibility timeouts), periodic heartbeat renewals, and monotonically increasing fencing tokens to prevent zombie workers from corrupting downstream state.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A Distributed Job Scheduler executes millions of recurring cron jobs and one-off delayed tasks with high accuracy, fault tolerance, and at-least-once execution guarantees.
bullets: Functional: Schedule one-off delayed jobs (e.g., execute at timestamp T) and recurring cron jobs (e.g., every Monday at 9 AM); support job cancellation, status querying, and configurable retry policies.
Functional: Provide task execution callbacks with execution history logs.
Non-Functional: Sub-second scheduling accuracy (jobs trigger within 1 second of their scheduled time).
Non-Functional: High scalability: support tens of millions of scheduled jobs with high execution throughput.
Non-Functional: Fault tolerance: no lost jobs during worker crashes or scheduler node failures.
Out of Scope: Complex DAG task workflow dependencies (handled by systems like Airflow/Temporal) and long-running distributed compute batch jobs (Spark/Hadoop).

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Job schedulers manage large volumes of quiescent future jobs punctuated by high execution peaks at round-hour boundaries.
bullets: Scheduled Inventory: 100 million total registered jobs stored in the system.
Execution Rate: 10 million jobs executed daily (~115 jobs/second average).
Peak Boundary Surges: Schedulers experience massive traffic spikes at round hours (e.g., midnight, top of the hour), peaking at 20,000 jobs/second.
Job Payload: Average job definition with parameters and metadata is ~1 KB. 100M jobs = ~100 GB of schedule storage.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Scanning 100 million rows every second to find due jobs destroys database performance. Time-bucketed partitioning is mandatory.
bullets: Why `SELECT ... WHERE trigger_time <= NOW()` fails: Running this query every second across 100M rows triggers continuous B-tree index traversals, lock contention, and high I/O wait.

Time-bucket partition sizing: Partition jobs into 1-minute buckets (`YYYY-MM-DD-HH-mm`). A minute with 20,000 jobs has a bucket size of ~20 MB. A scheduler node simply reads that single minute bucket in a sequential scan.
Timing wheel memory sizing: Loading 20,000 jobs into an in-memory timing wheel for sub-second precision consumes only a few megabytes of RAM.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Achieving sub-second scheduling accuracy across millions of jobs requires combining database time-bucketing with memory timing wheels.
bullets: Minute-level time bucketing: When a job is scheduled for 14:05:22, it is saved in bucket `2026-09-30-14-05`. At 14:04:45, a scanner node pulls all jobs for the `14-05` bucket into an in-memory Hierarchical Timing Wheel.

Hierarchical Timing Wheel (HashedWheelTimer): A circular buffer of 60 slots (one for each second of the minute). A background thread ticks every second, advancing the pointer and dispatching all jobs in that second's slot to Kafka.

Lease management and fencing tokens: When a worker pulls a job from Kafka, it acquires a lease with a 30-second visibility timeout and a monotonic fencing token. If the job takes 20 seconds, the worker sends a heartbeat to extend the lease. If the worker crashes, the lease expires and another worker picks up the job.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Handling missed executions during scheduler outages, preventing duplicate runs, and mitigating zombie workers ensures scheduling reliability.
bullets: Handling scheduler downtime (Catch-up scanner): If a scanner node crashes and restarts 5 minutes later, a Catch-Up Worker scans all minute buckets between the last checkpoint and the current time, executing missed jobs according to their misfire policy.

Zombie worker mitigation with fencing tokens: If Worker A encounters a long garbage collection pause, its lease expires and Worker B takes over the job with fencing token 42. When Worker A wakes up and attempts to commit results using token 41, the database rejects the write.

Idempotent job execution: Job payloads must include an `idempotency_key`. Workers pass this key to target APIs, ensuring that network retries or failover handoffs do not trigger duplicate side-effects.

tradeOffs.pros: Scales to hundreds of millions of jobs; sub-second scheduling precision; low database query overhead.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires in-memory buffering and careful state handoff during scanner node failover.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large-scale enterprise job schedulers (Airbnb Chronos, Uber Cherokee, cloud task runners).

tradeOffs.option: Continuous Database Polling (SELECT WHERE trigger <= NOW())
tradeOffs.pros: Simple to implement; purely stateless scheduler nodes.
tradeOffs.cons: Catastrophic database index lock contention; degrades rapidly past a few thousand scheduled tasks.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small internal tools or prototypes with low task counts (< 10,000 total jobs).

tradeOffs.option: Redis Sorted Sets (ZSET) for Delayed Scheduling
tradeOffs.pros: Fast O(log N) insertion and ZRANGEBYSCORE range queries; sub-10ms precision out of the box.
tradeOffs.cons: Memory-bound: storing millions of heavy job payloads in RAM is expensive compared to SSD storage.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Task queues with short-term delays (< 24 hours) like Celery, Sidekiq, or BullMQ.

subtopics.title: Metrics / Logging System
subtopics.subtitle: Observability platform architecture: Gorilla TSDB compression, inverted label indexes, and streaming alert evaluation.
keyTakeaways: Prevent high-cardinality tag explosions from exhausting TSDB memory: map unique label combinations to a 64-bit series_id using an Inverted Index (Roaring Bitmaps), and enforce per-tenant cardinality quotas at the ingestion gateway.

Achieve 10x-12x compression on time-series samples (16 bytes -> ~1.37 bytes per sample) using Facebook Gorilla encoding (Delta-of-Delta timestamps + XOR floating-point values) inside 2-hour immutable blocks.

Store logs cost-effectively (the Grafana Loki / ClickHouse pattern) by indexing only low-cardinality metadata labels (service, env, level) while streaming compressed log chunks directly to S3 with Bloom filters for fast needle-in-a-haystack substring searches.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A centralized Observability Platform (similar to Datadog or Prometheus + Loki) ingests, stores, and queries high-volume time-series metrics and structured logs from thousands of microservices with real-time alerting.
bullets: Functional: Ingest numeric time-series metrics (Counters, Gauges, Histograms) and structured JSON logs; provide fast PromQL/LogQL query capabilities for dashboards; evaluate alert rules continuously.
Functional: Support multi-tenancy with strict tag isolation and ingestion rate limiting.
Non-Functional: High write throughput (support 5 million metric samples/sec and 500,000 log events/sec).
Non-Functional: Sub-second dashboard query latency for common 24-hour time ranges.
Non-Functional: Extreme storage efficiency (under 2 bytes per metric sample on disk).
Out of Scope: Full APM distributed trace graph reconstruction (Jaeger/Tempo) and automated synthetic browser testing.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Observability infrastructure processes continuous, non-stop streams of machine-generated telemetry that surge during system outages.
bullets: Metrics Throughput: 5 million metric samples per second (~300 million samples/minute).
Active Time Series: 10 million distinct active time series across all monitored services.
Log Volume: 500,000 log events per second at 500 bytes per log = 250 MB/s of log ingestion (~21.6 TB/day).
Query Patterns: 95% of queries target telemetry generated within the past 24 hours; long-term queries run over downsampled aggregations.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations

bullets: Uncompressed metric volume: 5M samples/sec * 16 bytes (8-byte timestamp + 8-byte float value) = 80 MB/s = ~6.9 TB/day of raw numbers.
Gorilla compression savings: Gorilla XOR compression shrinks samples to ~1.4 bytes each: 5M samples * 1.4 bytes = ~7 MB/s = ~600 GB/day (over 90% reduction).
Log storage costs: 21.6 TB/day of raw JSON logs compressed via Zstandard (10x ratio) yields ~2.1 TB/day of compressed columnar blocks stored cheaply in S3.

Logs Ingestion: `POST /v1/logs/push` takes batches of `{ labels: {service, env}, lines: [{ ts, line, traceId }] }`.
Time Series Model: Metric series mapped to a unique 64-bit `SeriesID`. Inverted index maps `LabelKey=LabelValue` to a Roaring Bitmap of matching `SeriesID`s.
Chunk Storage: 2-hour compressed chunks holding 120 samples per series, flushed from memory to disk or S3.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The architecture decouples high-throughput ingestion gateways, in-memory TSDB head blocks, long-term object storage, and streaming alert engines.
bullets: Ingestion Gateway Fleet: Validates OTLP payloads, enforces label cardinality quotas, and publishes streams to Kafka.
TSDB Ingestion Nodes (Head Block): Holds the current 2-hour window of time series in memory using Gorilla compression, backed by a Write-Ahead Log (WAL).
Compactor & Downsampler: Merges expired 2-hour blocks into 24-hour Parquet blocks in S3 and computes 5-minute/1-hour rollups for long-term retention.
Query Engine (PromQL / LogQL): Fan-out querier that reads hot data from Ingestion Head blocks and historical data from S3 chunk storage.
Streaming Alert Evaluator: Evaluates PromQL SLO rules continuously against the live in-memory metric stream without querying disk.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Achieving sub-second queries across 10 million active series requires fast inverted index lookups and Gorilla compression algorithms.
bullets: Inverted index with Roaring Bitmaps: When a query requests `{service="checkout", status="500"}`, the engine looks up the bitmap of series IDs for `service="checkout"` and the bitmap for `status="500"`, performing a bitwise AND in CPU registers in microseconds to find matching series IDs.

Gorilla timestamp compression (Delta-of-Delta): Regular metrics arrive at fixed intervals (e.g., every 15s). The delta between timestamps is 15s, making the delta-of-delta zero. Gorilla encodes a zero delta-of-delta using a single bit `0`, consuming almost zero space for timestamps.

Gorilla value compression (XOR encoding): Floating-point metric values change little from sample to sample. XORing the current value with the previous value produces leading and trailing zeroes. Gorilla encodes only the meaningful bits between zeroes, shrinking 64-bit floats to an average of 1.1 bits per sample.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Protecting observability platforms from cardinality explosions, backpressure, and ingestion dropouts is critical during infrastructure incidents.
bullets: Tag cardinality circuit breakers: If a buggy deployment starts attaching `user_id` or raw query URLs as metric labels, the ingestion gateway detects that the metric's unique series count has exceeded 10,000. It rejects the new labels and triggers an alert, protecting the TSDB inverted index from memory exhaustion.

Downsampling for long-term retention: Raw 15-second metric samples are retained for 14 days. After 14 days, a background compactor downsamples the data to 5-minute averages, min, and max, and after 90 days downsamples to 1-hour rollups, cutting long-term storage costs by 95%.

Log label discipline (Loki model): Never index high-cardinality values (user IDs, IP addresses) in log metadata labels. Index only stable labels (`app`, `env`, `pod`), and rely on parallel brute-force grep across compressed S3 chunks for free-text substring searches.

tradeOffs.pros: 80-90% lower infrastructure cost than Elasticsearch; tiny index size; zero JVM heap pressure; easy scaling on S3.
tradeOffs.cons: Slow for unindexed ad-hoc text searches across wide multi-month time ranges.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume microservice application logs, VPC flow logs, and cloud-native Kubernetes platforms.

tradeOffs.pros: Sub-second needle-in-a-haystack searches across any arbitrary field, UUID, or stack trace substring.
tradeOffs.cons: Massive storage amplification (index is often 1.5x-2x larger than raw log data); expensive RAM requirements.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Security incident forensics, compliance audit trails, and low-to-medium log volume systems.

tradeOffs.pros: Pull controls scrape backpressure and automatically discovers dead pods; push works seamlessly with serverless and firewalled networks.
tradeOffs.cons: Pull requires direct network connectivity to application pods; push can overwhelm collectors during retry storms.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Use Pull for long-running Kubernetes pods; use Push for serverless lambdas and edge IoT devices.

subtopics.title: YouTube / Video Streaming
subtopics.subtitle: Video streaming platform: resumable chunked uploads, DAG transcoding, ABR packaging, and edge CDN delivery.
keyTakeaways: Never process raw multi-gigabyte video uploads as a single monolithic file: use S3 presigned multipart uploads and split video files at Group-of-Pictures (GOP) keyframe boundaries so worker clusters can transcode 4-second chunks in parallel.

Deliver smooth playback over fluctuating cellular networks using Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) streaming (HLS / DASH): client players measure buffer health and network throughput to switch dynamically between 360p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K at chunk boundaries.

Apply multi-tier CDN storage: cache the top 5% viral videos on edge NVMe SSDs near users, keep the next 20% in regional origin shields, and store long-tail archival videos in cold cloud object storage.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A global Video Streaming Platform allows creators to upload high-definition video files, transcodes them into multiple resolutions, and streams them reliably to millions of concurrent viewers worldwide.
bullets: Functional: Resumable chunked video upload; asynchronous transcoding into multiple resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K); Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) streaming playback.
Functional: Video metadata management (title, description, tags, view count) and thumbnail extraction.
Non-Functional: Sub-2 second video startup latency; minimal buffering during playback over fluctuating mobile connections.
Non-Functional: High durability for uploaded master videos (99.999999999% via cloud object storage).
Out of Scope: Live streaming real-time WebRTC ingest, automated copyrighted content fingerprint matching, and real-time ad insertion auctions.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Video platforms have massive storage and egress bandwidth demands driven by asymmetric upload vs view ratios.
bullets: Upload Volume: 500 hours of video uploaded every minute (~30,000 hours/hour, or ~720,000 hours/day).
Viewer Volume: 1 billion daily active views averaging 10 minutes of watch time = 10 billion minutes of video streamed/day.
Storage Ingestion: Average raw upload bitrate = 20 Mbps (~9 GB/hour). Daily master storage ingest = 720,000 * 9 GB = ~6.48 PB/day.
Transcoded Storage: Transcoding into 4 resolutions (360p, 720p, 1080p, 4K) adds ~4x storage overhead, requiring ~25 PB of new storage daily.
Egress Bandwidth: 10 billion minutes/day at average 3 Mbps streaming bitrate = ~3.75 Tbps of continuous outbound CDN bandwidth.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Bandwidth and storage calculations demonstrate why video platforms rely completely on distributed edge CDNs and chunk-level transcoding pipelines.
bullets: Egress bandwidth scale: 10 billion minutes / 86,400 seconds = ~115,000 concurrent streaming hours per second. At 3 Mbps average bitrate = ~345 Gbps baseline, peaking at 1.5 to 2 Tbps during peak evening hours.
CDN offload requirement: No origin data center can afford 2 Tbps of direct egress. The edge CDN must achieve a 95%+ Cache Hit Ratio (CHR) to keep origin traffic under 100 Gbps.
Transcoding compute sizing: Transcoding 720,000 hours of video daily within 24 hours requires a distributed fleet capable of processing 30,000 hours of video per hour in parallel.

sections.body: Video APIs must support multipart resumable upload sessions, manifest retrieval, and metadata queries.
bullets: Upload Initiation: `POST /v1/videos/upload-session` returns `{ uploadId, presignedChunkUrls: [...] }`.
Playback API: `GET /v1/videos/{videoId}/master.m3u8` returns the HLS master playlist referencing sub-playlists for 360p, 720p, 1080p, and 4K.
Metadata Schema (PostgreSQL/CockroachDB): Stores `video_id`, `uploader_id`, `title`, `duration`, `status` (`UPLOADING`, `TRANSCODING`, `READY`), and manifest URLs.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The video architecture separates the ingestion and transcoding pipeline from the streaming CDN delivery path.
bullets: Upload Service: Generates S3 presigned multipart URLs so client mobile devices upload chunks directly to S3 buckets, bypassing application servers.
Transcoding Orchestrator (DAG Pipeline): Triggers on S3 upload completion, splits raw video into 4-second GOP chunks, and schedules parallel FFmpeg tasks.
Transcoding Worker Fleet: Spot/Preemptible GPU instances running containerized FFmpeg workers that output fragmented MP4 (fMP4) chunks.
Storage Tier: Cloud object storage (S3) holding master videos, video segments, and `.m3u8` playlist files.
Global CDN Tier: Edge POPs that cache 4-second video segments close to viewers worldwide.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Transcoding multi-gigabyte videos sequentially takes hours. Splitting videos into independent keyframe chunks enables near-real-time parallel processing.
bullets: GOP (Group of Pictures) chunking: A video consists of keyframes (I-frames) followed by delta frames (P/B-frames). Split the master file strictly at I-frame boundaries into 4-second segments so each chunk can be decoded and encoded independently.

Parallel DAG transcoding: A 60-minute video yields 900 chunks. Distribute the 900 chunks across 100 worker containers. All chunks transcode in parallel within 2 to 3 minutes, followed by a stitcher step that writes the master HLS manifest.

Adaptive Bitrate (ABR) switching: The client video player monitors download speed and buffer fullness. If buffer health drops below 4 seconds, the player switches to downloading the 720p chunk instead of 1080p, preventing playback stalls.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Optimizing CDN cache efficiency and handling spot instance interruptions are central to video platform economics.
bullets: Spot instance termination handling: Transcoding workers run on cheap cloud Spot/Preemptible instances. Because chunks are small (4 seconds), if a spot instance is reclaimed, the orchestrator simply reschedules that single chunk on another worker.

Pre-warming video manifests: When a video from a popular creator goes live, push the master playlist and first three 4-second chunks to regional CDN edge caches before notifying subscribers, eliminating the initial stampede on origin storage.
Tiered storage lifecycle: After 30 days, move master raw upload files to cold archival storage (Glacier), keeping only optimized ABR chunks on standard object storage.

tradeOffs.pros: Massive parallelization; a 2-hour 4K video transcodes in minutes; spot instance reclaims only drop a 4-second task.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires complex DAG orchestration and precise I-frame boundary splitting logic.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Large-scale video platforms (YouTube, Netflix, Vimeo) processing thousands of hours daily.

tradeOffs.pros: Simple architecture; run FFmpeg directly on a single large compute instance.
tradeOffs.cons: Takes hours for long videos; if the instance crashes at 98%, the entire transcoding job must restart from scratch.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Small internal video tools or low-traffic platforms with short (< 2 minute) video clips.

tradeOffs.option: Direct S3 Presigned Uploads vs Gateway Proxying
tradeOffs.pros: Client uploads go directly to object storage; zero upload bandwidth or memory overhead on application servers.
tradeOffs.cons: Requires client-side multipart chunk management and S3 webhook integration for upload completion.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Any production platform handling user-generated video or large file uploads.

subtopics.interviewTip: Never propose uploading or transcoding a 10 GB video file as a single monolithic unit. Explain how S3 presigned multipart uploads handle the upload, and how splitting the video at GOP (Group of Pictures) boundaries allows hundreds of worker containers to transcode chunks in parallel.

subtopics.title: Rate Limiter
subtopics.subtitle: Distributed API rate limiting: Redis Lua scripts, Token Bucket algorithms, and low-latency gateway integration.
keyTakeaways: The Token Bucket algorithm is the production standard for API gateways: it allows controlled bursts up to bucket capacity while enforcing a steady refill rate using only two fields per key (tokens and lastRefillTimestamp).
Race conditions in distributed rate limiters must be eliminated by executing the token refill and decrement logic inside an atomic Redis Lua script (EVALSHA).
A production rate limiter must fail open (or fall back to local in-memory token buckets) during Redis partitions to prevent a monitoring tool from taking down the entire API.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: An API Rate Limiter tracks request frequency per client (user ID, IP address, API key) and throttles excess traffic to protect backends from overload and abuse.
bullets: Functional: Support multi-tier limits (e.g., 100 req/min for free users, 5,000 req/min for enterprise tiers, 20 req/sec per IP).
Functional: Return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) with `Retry-After`, `X-RateLimit-Limit`, and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers.
Non-Functional: Sub-2ms decision latency. Because the rate limiter sits on the critical request path, it must not become a performance bottleneck.
Non-Functional: Resilient fail-open behavior: if the rate-limiter cluster goes dark, customer traffic must continue to flow to backends.
Out of Scope: Payment collection for API upgrades, bot CAPTCHA challenges, and deep payload inspection for SQL injection.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Because rate limiters inspect every inbound request, their throughput directly matches total ingress platform volume.
bullets: Throughput: 100,000 requests per second across the API gateway, peaking at 250,000 RPS during major promotions.
Key Cardinality: 10 million daily active API keys / IP addresses tracked simultaneously.

Memory Footprint: Each rate-limit entry requires roughly 64 bytes (key name, token count, last refill timestamp). 10 million active keys * 64 bytes = ~640 MB of RAM, easily fitting in a modest Redis cluster.
Latency Budget: The rate limiter must execute in under 2ms (p99) to keep total gateway overhead within acceptable bounds.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Calculating Redis memory and network throughput proves that memory capacity is negligible, but Redis command throughput (IOPS) requires horizontal sharding.
bullets: Redis IOPS sizing: A single Redis thread processes ~80,000 to 100,000 ops/second under pipelined workloads. Handling 250,000 peak RPS requires a Redis Cluster with at least 4 to 6 master nodes.
Network bandwidth: 250,000 RPS * 128 bytes per Redis command/response = ~32 MB/s of network transfer, well within standard cloud VPC limits.
Memory retention: Keys expire automatically via TTL (e.g., 2 * refill period), preventing inactive users from accumulating stale entries in Redis memory.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: The rate limiter operates primarily as an Envoy or API Gateway middleware filter, returning standard RFC-compliant HTTP headers on every evaluated request.
bullets: Middleware contract: `checkRateLimit(clientId, cost=1)` returns `{ allowed: boolean, remainingTokens, resetTimeMs }`.
HTTP response headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit: 1000`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 842`, `X-RateLimit-Reset: 1727788800`.
Redis Hash data model: Key: `rate:{tier}:{clientId}`, Fields: `tokens` (float) and `last_refill_ts` (integer epoch ms).

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: Rate limiting can be evaluated at the edge proxy (Envoy), inside centralized rate-limit microservices, or directly within application middleware.
bullets: Edge Gateway (Envoy / Kong): Intercepts the request and invokes a local or external rate limit service before routing to backend microservices.
Distributed Cache (Redis Cluster): Stores token state per client, partitioned across nodes using consistent hash slots (`{clientId}`).
In-Process L1 Token Bucket: For high-traffic bot endpoints, a lightweight in-memory bucket absorbs massive single-IP floods before they reach Redis.
Asynchronous Metric Reporter: Streams dropped request counts to Prometheus to trigger alerts when error rates spike.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Implementing distributed rate limiting with separate Redis `GET` and `SET` commands creates race conditions where concurrent requests overwrite token counters.
bullets: The check-then-set race condition: Two concurrent requests read tokens = 1 simultaneously. Both conclude they can proceed, decrement tokens to 0, and write back to Redis. Both requests succeed, violating the rate limit.

Atomic Lua execution: Encapsulate the refill math and decrement operation inside an atomic Redis Lua script executed via `EVALSHA`. Redis guarantees that no other command executes concurrently on that key.

Sliding Window Counter vs Token Bucket: Token Bucket is ideal for burst-tolerant API gateways. Sliding Window Log provides exact precision for payment transactions but consumes significantly more memory (storing timestamps of every request in a Redis Sorted Set).

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: The rate limiter must never become the cause of an application outage. Robust degradation strategies are mandatory.
bullets: Fail-Open on Redis timeout: If the Redis command exceeds a 5ms timeout or the cluster is unreachable, log an error, increment a fallback metric, and allow the request through.
Local circuit breaking: When Redis health drops below acceptable thresholds, trip a circuit breaker and evaluate limits using local in-process token buckets on each gateway node.

Multi-region synchronization: Do not attempt synchronous cross-region replication for rate-limit tokens—the speed-of-light WAN latency is too high. Instead, divide global quotas across regions (e.g., 50% US, 50% EU) or run local rate limiters per region.

tradeOffs.option: Token Bucket via Redis Lua Script
tradeOffs.pros: Atomic execution; supports smooth traffic bursts; constant O(1) time and tiny memory footprint (2 numbers per key).
tradeOffs.cons: Does not enforce uniform spacing between requests during burst phases.
tradeOffs.bestFor: General API gateways, public REST APIs, and microservice ingress protection.

tradeOffs.pros: Mathematically exact rate enforcement; prevents boundary doubling attacks at the turn of a minute.
tradeOffs.cons: High memory usage (stores a timestamp per request); unbounded memory growth under denial-of-service floods.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Sensitive endpoints with low rate limits (login attempts, password resets, SMS verification).

tradeOffs.option: Local In-Memory Limiting vs Centralized Redis
tradeOffs.pros: Sub-millisecond local execution; zero network overhead; immune to centralized Redis outages.
tradeOffs.cons: Limits are per-instance rather than global; adding gateway pods effectively increases total allowed platform traffic.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Protecting against sudden volumetric DDoS attacks at the ingress edge.

subtopics.interviewTip: Explain why separate GET and SET commands fail under concurrency due to race conditions. Show how an atomic Redis Lua script executes the token refill and decrement in a single step, and explain why the gateway must fail open if Redis becomes unreachable.

keyTakeaways: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes limits key remapping to ~1/N of the keyspace when cache nodes join or leave, preventing cache-miss avalanches against backend databases.
Inside individual cache nodes, pairing concurrent hash lookups with segmented eviction lists (or W-TinyLFU) achieves O(1) performance without global lock contention across CPU cores.
Defend against the three classic cache failure modes: Cache Stampede (Singleflight coalescing), Cache Penetration (Bloom filters / negative caching), and Hot Keys (L1 near-cache).

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A Distributed Cache stores high-frequency data in memory across a cluster of nodes, reducing backend database load and delivering sub-millisecond read latencies.
bullets: Functional: Support `GET(key)`, `SET(key, value, ttl)`, and `DEL(key)` operations across a cluster of storage nodes.
Functional: Configurable eviction policies (LRU, LFU, FIFO) to reclaim memory when cache nodes reach capacity.
Non-Functional: Sub-millisecond read latency (p99 < 1ms on local network) with high horizontal read scalability.
Non-Functional: High availability with automatic shard rebalancing when cache nodes fail or scale up.
Out of Scope: Persistent ACID transactional ledgers, cross-datacenter multi-region consensus, and complex secondary index queries.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: A large-scale caching tier handles heavy read throughput with strict latency constraints.
bullets: Throughput: 1,000,000 read QPS and 50,000 write QPS across the cluster.
Data Size: 100 million active items with an average object size of 5 KB = ~500 GB of raw cached data.
Cluster Sizing: Sizing with 2x memory headroom for fragmentation and eviction buffers yields ~1 TB of cluster RAM, distributed across 16 nodes with 64 GB RAM each.
Network Throughput: 1,000,000 reads/sec * 5 KB = 5 GB/s of egress bandwidth across the cluster (~312 MB/s per node, requiring 10 Gbps network interfaces).

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Calculating memory and network requirements shows that distributed caches are typically network-bound or CPU-bound rather than memory-constrained.
bullets: Memory sizing: 100M items * (5 KB payload + 64 bytes metadata) = ~506 GB. Budgeting 1 TB allows for hot-key redundancy and overhead.
Node count calculation: 16 cache nodes provide 1 TB of total RAM and aggregate network bandwidth of 160 Gbps, comfortably absorbing 40 Gbps of read traffic.
Eviction rate: At 50,000 writes/sec with full memory, the cluster evicts ~50,000 old keys/sec, making low-overhead eviction algorithms essential.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Use lightweight binary protocols (like Redis RESP or Memcached binary protocol) over persistent TCP/gRPC connections to minimize serialization overhead.
bullets: Wire protocol: Binary commands for `GET`, `SET`, `MGET`, and `DELETE` with explicit 32-bit TTL values and integer payload lengths.
Internal node storage: Keys and values stored in contiguous off-heap memory buffers or slab allocators to minimize garbage collection pauses.
Metadata headers: 16 bytes per entry storing TTL expiration timestamp, LRU pointers, and frequency counts.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The caching architecture combines smart client routing, a distributed hashing ring, and node-level memory engines.
bullets: Smart Client Routing: Clients maintain a local view of the consistent hash ring, hashing keys directly to target nodes without intermediate proxy hops.
Consistent Hash Ring (ZooKeeper / Gossip): Discovers node health and maintains virtual node assignments across the hash circle.
Cache Worker Node: Runs multi-threaded network event loops (epoll/kqueue) reading from segregated in-memory partitions.
L1 Near-Cache: A small in-process cache inside application pods that absorbs ultra-hot keys with short 1-second TTLs.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: A distributed cache must route keys efficiently and evict data without letting locks stall request threads.
bullets: Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes: Map nodes to multiple points (e.g., 256 vnodes per server) on a 2^32 integer ring. When a server fails, its keys are redistributed evenly across all remaining servers rather than overloading a single neighbor.

Segmented LRU and W-TinyLFU: Traditional LRU suffers from cache pollution when a sequential batch scan flushes out popular items. W-TinyLFU uses a Bloom filter-like Count-Min Sketch to admit new keys only if their frequency exceeds the eviction candidate.
Lock-free eviction: Partition the cache into independent segments (like Java's `ConcurrentHashMap`), each with its own eviction list, eliminating cross-core lock contention.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Production caching failures frequently cascade into database outages. Defensive mechanisms are required to keep the storage tier safe.
bullets: Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd): When a hot key expires, thousands of concurrent requests miss and query the database simultaneously. Solve this using Singleflight request coalescing (only one thread fetches from the database while others await the result) and probabilistic early recomputation (XFetch).

Cache Penetration: Requests for non-existent keys bypass the cache and hit the database directly. Use a Bloom filter at the cache layer to reject invalid keys, or cache null values with a short 30-second TTL.
Hot Key Mitigation: Replicate ultra-popular keys across multiple nodes by appending random suffixes (`item_123#1`, `item_123#2`) or serving them from in-process L1 memory.

tradeOffs.option: Smart Client Routing (Direct to Cache Node)
tradeOffs.pros: Zero proxy hop latency; sub-millisecond response times; no central load balancer bottleneck.
tradeOffs.cons: Clients must maintain cluster topology state; updating the hash ring requires notifying all clients.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput internal microservices with low latency budgets (Memcached, Redis Cluster clients).

tradeOffs.pros: Clients remain simple and stateless; centralized connection pooling and security enforcement.
tradeOffs.cons: Adds 0.5 to 1ms of extra network hop latency; proxy tier requires separate scaling and maintenance.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Polyglot environments where maintaining smart client libraries in multiple languages is impractical.

tradeOffs.pros: W-TinyLFU delivers 10 to 20% higher hit ratios by resisting cache pollution from one-off sequential scans.
tradeOffs.cons: Slightly higher CPU overhead for frequency tracking compared to a basic doubly-linked LRU list.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Modern production caches with mixed read/scan workloads (Caffeine, Redis 6+ LFU).

subtopics.interviewTip: When asked how to prevent cache stampedes, explain Singleflight coalescing: only one request goes to the database while others wait on a shared channel. Combine this with consistent hashing virtual nodes to explain how the cluster survives node additions and failures.

subtopics.title: Notification System
subtopics.subtitle: Multi-channel notification architecture: APNs/FCM push, SMS, email, priority isolation, and rate-limit backpressure.
keyTakeaways: Isolate high-priority transactional alerts (two-factor OTPs, fraud warnings) from low-priority marketing blasts using dedicated Kafka topics and worker pools so a 20M-user campaign never delays a login code.

Third-party delivery providers (Apple APNs, Google FCM, Twilio, SendGrid) have variable latencies and strict rate limits: workers must decouple ingestion from dispatch using dead-letter queues and tiered retry topics with exponential backoff.

Guarantee at-least-once delivery without duplicate user alerts by enforcing an idempotencyKey at the API gateway and checking a short-lived Redis deduplication key immediately before dispatching to external providers.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A centralized Notification Platform ingests event notifications from internal microservices and dispatches them across mobile push, SMS, and email while respecting user preferences, rate limits, and quiet hours.
bullets: Functional: Deliver multi-channel notifications (Push via APNs/FCM, SMS via Twilio, Email via SendGrid/SES); support transactional and marketing classifications.
Functional: User preference management (opt-out of marketing, channel preference, time-zone aware quiet hours); deduplication of repeated events.
Non-Functional: High throughput (support 50 million notifications/day) with low latency for transactional events (OTP delivery p99 < 5 seconds).
Non-Functional: At-least-once delivery with near-zero duplicate alerts experienced by end users.
Out of Scope: WYSIWYG email template authoring tools, SMS conversation two-way replying, and user-to-user in-app chat.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Notification platforms handle a mix of steady transactional traffic and massive bursts during scheduled marketing campaigns.
bullets: Daily Volume: 50 million notifications per day (~600 notifications/second average).
Peak Blast Rate: Marketing flash sales generate bursts of up to 50,000 notifications/second.
Channel Breakdown: 65% Mobile Push (APNs/FCM), 25% Email, 10% SMS.
Payload Sizing: Average notification payload is ~1 KB of JSON. 50 million * 1 KB = 50 GB/day of message data.
Downstream Constraints: Twilio SMS accounts are throttled (e.g., 100-200 SMS/sec); SendGrid enforces account-level concurrency limits.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Capacity planning centers around message broker throughput, worker thread sizing, and protecting downstream vendor rate limits.
bullets: Kafka partition sizing: 50,000 peak msgs/sec with a target of ~1,000 msgs/sec per partition requires at least 50 partitions on the high-throughput marketing topic.

Worker fleet sizing: If an external APNs/FCM HTTP/2 call takes an average of 50ms, one worker thread handles 20 deliveries/second. Delivering 10,000 push/sec requires 500 concurrent worker threads (or non-blocking async event loops).
Redis deduplication storage: Storing 50 million notification keys for 24 hours (key: `notif:dedup:{userId}:{eventId}`, 40 bytes) requires ~2.5 GB of Redis RAM.

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: The ingestion API must accept notifications synchronously with minimal latency, returning an acknowledgment immediately while processing delivery asynchronously.
bullets: Ingestion API: `POST /v1/notifications/send` takes `{ recipientUserId, templateId, channel, priority: "HIGH"|"LOW", idempotencyKey, templateParams }` and returns `{ notificationId, status: "QUEUED" }`.
User Preferences Schema: PostgreSQL table storing user channel toggles, unsubscribed categories, and quiet-hour time windows.

Notification Log Schema: Cassandra or DynamoDB table partitioned by `(user_id, date)` recording delivery attempt timestamps, external provider message IDs, and terminal status (`DELIVERED`, `BOUNCED`, `FAILED`).
